rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of conventional piety and prophetic/poetic assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular religion and poetry are accused of portraying justice/virtue as instruments for gaining divine favor (material blessings, long posterity) or for avoiding underworld punishments via rituals; these portrayals encourage appearances-over-substance morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates and interlocutors treat such conventional assurances as insufficient grounds for affirming justice's intrinsic value and urge inquiry into the true effect of justice on the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as essentially ideal and generic
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, 'as poetry, is essentially ideal, that it avoids and excludes all accident; that its apparent individualities ... must be representative of a class.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should embody generic, class-representative attributes rather than eccentricities of a single individual. The poetic person must be clothed with common attributes of the class that make them typical and useful for poetic purpose. Anti-pattern: undue emphasis on accidental individual detail that undermines the poem's representative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public order and obedience to law
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The fundamental duty of a government is to preserve order, to enforce obedience of the laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat preservation of order as essential; disorder undermines legitimate demands and risks civil calamity. Guardians of order should include the sober poor as well as the rich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases
rubrics_metrics.description: general account; of walls, piers, shafts; decoration; faults of Gothic profiles; should not be richly decorated; general effect
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge bases for proportion, appropriate ornamentation level (avoid excess), family/type, and their contribution to overall massing (i.63-64; i.88; i.277-288; ii.386).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to enact central, essential affairs rather than merely describe them
rubrics_metrics.description: For the crucial matters of the story—changes of character, pivotal emotional events—prefer enactment (scenic drama) over mere pictorial report to achieve intensity and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'central, essential, paramount affair' should be dramatized; otherwise something is lost if it is represented solely by the hero’s account. Reserve scenes for such purposes rather than allowing continuous narration to dilute impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction genres sought
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction: Contemporary drama, sagas, psychological suspense, crime and thrillers, historical, literary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists these specific fiction subgenres as what Pan Macmillan Australia is currently seeking (i.e., preferred submissions should fit one of these categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronies (analepses and prolepses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective and anticipatory displacements of narrative order: analepses (retrospection) and prolepses (anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify these as departures from chronological (diegetic) order. Use them to map how the narrative rearranges events in telling; they are one constitutive feature of narrative temporality but not the whole story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion E: Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses clarity, accuracy, register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 1: Frequent inaccuracies; unclear
Level 2: (implied) limited clarity/accuracy
Level 3: (implied) generally clear and accurate
Level 4: (implied) clear, accurate, appropriate register
Level 5: Clear, varied, sophisticated; appropriate register; accurate vocabulary
(Evaluates correctness and stylistic quality of expression, including register and vocabulary choice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor, satire, and ironic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Blend comic exaggeration, ironic asides, and satirical observations about manners, customs, and national character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comic account of a funeral as festival with ‘not above a hundred gallons of whisky’ drunk; ironic national comparisons and playful hyperbole about longevity (Mackcrain 180 years). Use wit to keep tone lively and to critique or humanize subjects. Anti-pattern: flat seriousness where levity would illuminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and Figures of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful metaphor and figures are essential to striking expression and to revealing truth poetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective metaphors illuminate and fuse image with idea; avoid mixed or strained figures. Figures should be natural to the thought and strengthen precision and vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative — Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The text sets up a story by introducing the event/conflict, characters, and setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
5 Exceptional: The text creatively engages the reader by setting out a well-developed conflict, situation, or observation and its significance. It establishes one or multiple points of view and introduces a narrator and/or well-developed characters.
4 Skilled: The text engages and orients the reader by setting out a conflict, situation, or observation and its significance. It establishes one or multiple points of view and introduces a narrator and/or developed characters.
3 Proficient: The text orients the reader by setting out a conflict, situation, or observation and its significance. It establishes one point of view and introduces a narrator and/or developed characters.
2 Developing: The text provides a setting with a vague conflict, situation, or observation and its significance and introduces an underdeveloped narrator and/or characters.
1 Inadequate: The text provides a setting that is unclear with a vague conflict, situation, or observation and introduces an undeveloped narrator and/or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works posted with permission: comply with additional copyright-holder terms (1.E.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an individual Project Gutenberg work is posted with the permission of the copyright holder, your use and distribution must comply with 1.E.1–1.E.7 AND any additional terms imposed by the copyright holder (these additional terms will be linked to the Project Gutenberg License).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work includes a copyright-holder notice, read and follow both the full Project Gutenberg License and any extra conditions specified by the rights holder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher eligibility (press type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books must be published by commercial, university, or independent presses in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books that are self-published, or published by presses that charge for production or editorial services, are not eligible. This implies the press should be a legitimate U.S. publisher that does not require authors to pay for production/editorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit thoroughly to tighten prose, fix pacing, and polish the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Editing lesson and workbook exercises guide revision practices. Patterson's Office Hours critiques model blunt, constructive editing feedback. Focus editing on clarity, pacing, and removing unnecessary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refine Passions to Greater Elegance (transformative power of beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a third thing which may contribute ... and that is refining our Passions to a greater Elegance, than we receive them from Nature. When the Passion is Love, this Work is performed in innocent, though rude and uncultivated Minds, by the mere Force and Dignity of the Object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray love and other passions as capable of moral refinement when directed by noble objects; example: Dryden's Cymon and Iphigenia where beauty ennobles a rustic fool. As a writer, show character transformation credibly through encounters with dignified forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of critics' pedantry and received maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is described as easily accessible and prone to repetition of received opinions: critics repeat maxims (e.g., 'copy nature', 'art of blotting', 'keep nine years') and often form judgements from books and coffee-house talk rather than original insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should treat critics' pronouncements with caution — critics can be inconsistent, enamoured of rules, and influenced by fashion. Evaluate criticism for substance rather than authority or jargon (illustrated by the satirical figure Dick Minim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's imitation and end (evoking terror and pity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of terrible and pitiful things and ought to excite Terror and Compaſſion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of tragedy is to arouse these passions and thereby refine or purge them; subjects and presentation should be chosen to achieve those effects rather than to produce horror or mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between topography/material detail and informing light or expression
rubrics_metrics.description: In landscape and setting, the informing effect of light or an indwelling expression can unite otherwise commonplace material into a dominant artistic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether topography is modulated by light and mood (e.g., French riverside vs Swiss valley, Venetian landscape retaining abstract elements) so that material details serve the overall pictorial music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure meaningfulness through relevant examples and choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning materials should include examples that relate to learners and assignments that allow choice of meaningful activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize content with learner-relevant examples and design projects that permit personalization and real-world relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine methods of successful novelists and notice their devices
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us very carefully follow the methods of the novelists whose effects are incontestable, noticing exactly the manner in which the scenes and figures in their books are presented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study episodes to see what arts and devices produce relief, vividness, and intelligibility (how an episode is given relief, how a character is made vivid), and transfer those observations into critical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and unity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: In a word, be your subject what it will, let it be merely simple and uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patchwork, over-ambitious mixtures or subject-hopping (likened to a picture with mismatched parts). Keep a single coherent focus rather than fusing incongruous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and prosodic intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ear for music, and the 'power of approximating the varieties of poetical to those of musical rhythm,' shaping line-sound to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether lineation, rhythm, and sound reinforce sense; Milton's blank verse molds sound to image (lines rise/fall/pause appropriately). Anti-pattern: metrical patterns that obscure or contradict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter XXXVIII Q1
rubrics_metrics.description: What question was exciting the people of North Carolina at this period? What was thought of the Confederation?

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive understanding of the virtues in perfected form
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not behold 'the outline merely' of virtues like justice and temperance; 'nothing short of the most finished picture should satisfy us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must lead to a refined, precise grasp of the virtues—'highest accuracy'—not a crude or popular exposition. The standard demands full, nuanced understanding rather than approximate or folk definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting to agents/editors who accept direct submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agent/editor includes their submissions email or accepts direct submissions, you should go to their agency/publisher site, look up their submission guidelines, and follow those guidelines—usually an emailed query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave your pitch in the ManuscriptWishList comments; the site will not post pitches and the agent/editor will not see them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land use
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakdown of land by major uses (arable land, permanent crops, other) with percentages and year of estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide percents and date of data (e.g., 'arable land: 12.31%; permanent crops: 0.48%; other: 87.21% (2001)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate local lore and human history
rubrics_metrics.description: Weave myths, place-names, and local anecdotes into the natural description to enrich cultural resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau includes Indian fable about Walden's naming, the old log canoe, and villagers' memories. Such elements situate the landscape in human time and make the place layered and storied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative vividness and balance between thought and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: When ideas are vivid and there exists an endless power of combining and modifying them, feelings blend more easily with ideal creations than with sensory objects; minds so constituted are affected by thoughts rather than by things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imaginative power by the vividness and combinatory richness of ideas and by how feelings integrate with those ideas. Beware poets whose imaginative life is deficient and who therefore over-rely on immediate sensory impressions (which may lead to superstition or fanaticism). The 'sanity' of poetic imagination lies between superstition/fanaticism and indifference/lack of creative impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Making of Inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods and pitfalls in inferring causes, intentions, and facts from observed phenomena and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between observation and inference; apply rules of logic, probability, and analogy carefully; be alert to false causal leaps and confirmation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of mercantile system privileging producers over consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile laws often sacrifice consumers’ interest to producers’ interest — restraints on importation, bounties on exportation, and colonial monopolies burden home consumers with higher prices and the costs of empire (defence and debt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation: one should account for the full fiscal and welfare costs (e.g., wars and debts to maintain colonies) when judging claimed benefits to producers; small producer gains rarely offset large consumer and fiscal costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Consistency, Propriety, and Likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be believable and consistent, acting in ways appropriate to their nature and role in the plot; they should reflect types rather than implausible extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters need not be morally perfect; their actions must be intelligible within the story’s moral world and necessary for plot development. Avoid sudden, inexplicable changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should suggest life rather than slavishly reproduce speech; it must reveal character and advance the story while remaining intelligible and purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge dialogue by how much it reveals indirectly—social position, education, temperament—without becoming mere exposition. Avoid transcript-like realism that burdens the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness of art over mere phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations of art are more expressive and transparent than the phenomena of the real world; the mind finds it easier to penetrate works of art than raw natural events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong artwork clarifies and concentrates meaning; evaluators should look for economy and clarity of representation that make inner truth more accessible than in unmediated reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and word-formation — favor concise words; avoid excessive agglutination
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid artificial compound-agglutinated words where the language's stage of formation makes them awkward; concise, shorter words often produce superior poetic diction (as Virgil exemplified by rejecting many compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare counts of words per line across poets (e.g., Virgil vs. Lucan or Statius); prefer clarity and shorter words unless common usage sanctions a compound. Be wary of forcing Grecian agglutination onto languages unsuited to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tube cultivation aseptic technique for fluid media
rubrics_metrics.description: Flame cotton-wool plugs of source and sterile tubes, sterilise platinum loop, avoid touching tube sides, withdraw a small portion of growth with cooled loop, emulsify in sterile bouillon, replug, sterilise loop, label with organism and date, then incubate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold tubes nearly horizontal and avoid capillary contamination; always cool the loop before touching medium; label immediately after inoculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective (typically first-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narrators are usually features of literary works written in the first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While most commonly first-person, the device can appear in other narrative modes and also in visual media (film and television). Consider how point of view limits or frames the narrator's knowledge and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build to a Crisis or Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning point where characters recognize something new or make crucial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise stakes steadily toward a decisive moment in which characters confront core conflicts and undergo recognition or change. The climax should be the logical culmination of prior choices and revelations, prompting irreversible action or understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sententious, oracular moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Too fond of uttering moral reflections in a style too sententious and oracular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral reflections should not be delivered as trite, overbearing pronouncements. The reviewer criticizes grandiose, 'oracular' maxims that have become banal, recommending restraint and freshness in moral commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories honored
rubrics_metrics.description: The Awards currently honor the best Fiction, Nonfiction, Poetry, Translated Literature, and Young People’s Literature, published each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although other categories have been recognized in the past, the current categories are those five; submissions should be made into the appropriate category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A section dedicated to plotting — arranging events so they arise from characters and moral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page only lists the heading; the book contains methods for constructing plot and ensuring causal logic.
